thread_analysis.thread_summary: Hoshiden Corporation (contacts Yusuke Nomura, Masaki Hori) works extensively with Allion (Itsuo Sakai, Toshitaka Mochizuki, Masaya Iida) on Bluetooth SIG certification for a wristband activity tracker (smartwatch) module supplied to OEM set makers, referencing a TDK Silmee W22-style existing registration as an early quoting template. The thread (captured across 3 progressively fuller message snapshots spanning August-November 2024) documents an extensive registration-strategy negotiation: module-vendor DN acquisition strategy for OEM supply, RF PHY test scope reduction for an SoC registered as Controller Subsystem, and a substantial cross-layer GAP/LL Consistency Check inconsistency requiring a creative two-stage registration strategy (module-level DN via real RF PHY test, then customer-side Include-without-modification) to avoid GAP-layer protocol testing realistically achievable only by the stack vendor — through to final RF testing, registration Submission, and Compliance Folder delivery.
all_questions_found: Does a 'Default' DN display or Q30-prefixed QDID cause any disadvantage, and what registration structure best serves OEM customers? (see thread_0266_case_01)
Can RF PHY test scope be reduced to only the PHY mode (1M) actually implemented? (see thread_0266_case_02)
How do we avoid GAP-layer protocol testing that only the stack vendor can realistically perform, given this QDID combination's inherent inconsistency? (see thread_0266_case_03)
thread_analysis.key_technical_discussion: This thread provides a deep view into post-July-2024 registration site mechanics for module vendors: how DN assignment behavior differs between single and combined QDID/DN Includes, why an SoC registered as Controller Subsystem (rather than its technically-appropriate Component category) still requires real RF PHY test confirmation scoped to actual implementation, and a sophisticated two-stage registration strategy (separate module DN registration via RF PHY test, then customer-side unmodified Include) to route around a GAP-layer cross-layer inconsistency that would otherwise require protocol-level testing beyond the module vendor's realistic capability.
thread_analysis.key_decision_logic: See thread_0266_case_01 through thread_0266_case_03 for the specific decision logic behind each question.
thread_analysis.risk_if_done_wrong: See thread_0266_case_01 through thread_0266_case_03 for specific risks.
thread_analysis.consulting_mistake: None identified — Allion's proposed two-stage registration strategy (case_03) demonstrates resourceful problem-solving that avoided forcing the customer into either an unworkable GAP-layer testing requirement or a DN-less registration that would have undermined their OEM supply value proposition.
thread_analysis.consulting_takeaway: For module vendors supplying OEM set makers, registration strategy should be evaluated not just for immediate registrability but for what it leaves the vendor able to offer downstream customers (a referenceable DN) — when a specific Controller+Host QDID combination's inherent cross-layer inconsistency would require unrealistic protocol-level testing, consider restructuring the registration sequence (separate module DN acquisition via real RF testing, then customer-side unmodified Include) rather than defaulting to a no-DN Declaration-equivalent path.
